title: High-fidelity Three-Dimensional Flow Field Reconstruction Driven by Turbulent Fluid Dynamics
authors: Hanlin Kong, Jianan Wei, Yuntian Chen, Yujia Wang, Wenguan Wang
abstract: High-fidelity three-dimensional turbulent flow fields are essential for scientific and engineering analyses, yet obtaining them through direct numerical simulation or high-resolution measurements remains expensive. Super-resolution reconstruction from coarse-grained data therefore offers a promising alternative, but remains fundamentally challenging because fine-scale structures are intrinsically three-dimensional and dynamically coupled across scales. Existing data-driven approaches still struggle to recover multiscale volumetric structures and their coherent temporal evolution. To address these limitations, we propose a turbulence-aware framework for time-resolved three-dimensional flow reconstruction. The framework couples a multiscale neural operator, designed to recover volumetric structures, with a state space model to promote temporal consistency in the reconstructed dynamics. In addition, Navier-Stokes residuals are incorporated as soft constraints to regularize the reconstruction toward physically plausible dynamics. A mixture-of-experts mechanism is also introduced to support unsupervised adaptation to unknown coarse-graining. Across evaluations on canonical turbulent systems and atmospheric reanalysis data, the proposed framework reduces reconstruction errors relative to learning-based and classical baselines, while better preserving multiscale spatial structure and coherent temporal evolution. These results validate the effectiveness of the proposed framework in reconstructing high-fidelity three-dimensional flow fields from coarse-grained data.

infographic.key_insight: A turbulence-aware 3D reconstruction framework combines multiscale neural operators, temporal state-space modeling, and physics-based residual constraints to recover high-fidelity flow fields from coarse data.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables cheaper, more accurate surrogate reconstruction of turbulent volumes for CFD analysis, monitoring, and downstream scientific or engineering decision-making.
method: Multiscale neural operator reconstructs volumetric fine-scale spatial structures from coarse-grained inputs.
State-space model enforces coherent time evolution across reconstructed flow snapshots.
Navier–Stokes residuals and a mixture-of-experts module add physical regularization and adaptivity to unknown coarse-graining.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports improved reconstruction error and better preservation of multiscale spatial structure and temporal coherence on canonical turbulent systems and atmospheric reanalysis data.
infographic.watch_item: Performance may depend on how well the model generalizes across different coarse-graining patterns and turbulence regimes, especially where physics residuals are only soft constraints.
infographic.paper_title: High-fidelity Three-Dimensional Flow Field Reconstruction Driven by Turbulent Fluid Dynamics

title: Some generalizations of the tornado model
authors: S. N. Artekha
abstract: A possible mechanism of tornado generation is associated with the Schwarzschild criterion for convective instability. The supercooled cloud-air mixture near the axis starts to descend and, due to the super adiabatic temperature gradient, the overheated near-surface air mass rises. The complete system of equations for full model includes equations for the stream function, for the azimuthal velocity component, and for the change in density. The refined model considers rotating convection within the framework of ideal hydrodynamics. The simplest model uses a separate equation for the stream function and can be applied to the initial stage of vortex generation. Within the framework of the simplest model, an analytical solution is combined from 8 linear dependencies by height. Rotation increases due to the conservation of angular momentum. Within the framework of the refined model, some unidirectional differential rotation arises, but it depends on boundary conditions (can be local). The full model studies the tornado development as rotating convection from the very beginning to the quasi-stationary stage. Velocity components increase in a coordinated manner. Two cases are considered: a single whirlwind and a two-eyed tornado. Radial flows converge towards the central part of the tornado near the earth surface, and there is an outflow from the "wall" to the axis and to the periphery near the top of the tornado. The maximum vertical velocity component is achieved at a certain radial distance at a certain height. The maximum azimuthal velocity component is achieved in the tornado "wall". Tornado generation criteria are discussed.

infographic.key_insight: The paper models tornado formation as rotating convection driven by convective instability, showing how angular momentum conservation and buoyancy can amplify vortex rotation from early development to quasi-stationary stages.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The results help explain when and how tornado-like vortices intensify, offering a physics-based framework for hazard modeling and for interpreting rotating convection in atmospheric-flow simulations.
method: Builds a hierarchy of models: a simplest stream-function model, a refined ideal-hydrodynamics rotating-convection model, and a full model with stream function, azimuthal velocity, and density evolution.
Derives an analytical early-stage solution from eight linear height-dependent segments.
Compares single-whirlwind and two-eyed tornado scenarios under different boundary conditions.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports analytical model solutions and qualitative flow structure analysis rather than experimental measurements or benchmark datasets.
infographic.watch_item: Predicted rotation and vortex structure can depend strongly on boundary conditions, so results may be local and not directly generalizable without calibration.
infographic.paper_title: Some generalizations of the tornado model

title: AI Meets Turbulence Modeling: Complex Systems Perspective
authors: Sharath S. Girimaji
abstract: Despite widespread enthusiasm, applying artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) to turbulence modeling has yielded only modest progress, primarily due to a lack of situation-aware deployment. Data-driven Reynolds-averaged Navier--Stokes (ML-RANS) closures frequently fail to generalize across diverse flow regimes, while scale-resolving simulations (SRS) remain computationally prohibitive. As a result, ML-RANS is often misapplied outside its domain of validity, and ML-SRS is unnecessarily deployed on flows fully amenable to RANS. To guide optimal AI/ML deployment, we propose a turbulence taxonomy map parameterized by degrees of freedom ($Re$) and the degree of non-equilibrium ($SK/ε$). By applying Weaver's well-recognized complexity framework, we classify turbulence into distinct physical regimes. This categorization identifies where local ML-RANS surrogates can generalize, clarifies where explicit scale resolution is physically mandatory, and highlights where physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) are most effective. Ultimately, this perspective establishes a physics-grounded framework for the flow-aware, successful deployment of AI/ML in turbulence.

infographic.key_insight: The paper argues that AI/ML for turbulence works best when matched to the flow’s complexity regime, not applied generically across all turbulent flows.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A flow-aware turbulence taxonomy can help engineers choose between ML-RANS, scale-resolving simulation, and PINNs more effectively, avoiding both overuse and misuse of expensive models.
method: Map turbulence using two axes: Reynolds number (Re) and non-equilibrium level (Sk/ε).
Apply Weaver’s complexity framework to classify flows into distinct physical regimes.
Use the regime map to identify where ML-RANS can generalize, where explicit scale resolution is required, and where PINNs are most suitable.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract synthesizes prior AI/ML turbulence experience and reports that ML-RANS often fails to generalize while SRS is computationally prohibitive, motivating the proposed taxonomy rather than presenting new simulation data.
infographic.watch_item: The framework is conceptual and depends on correctly identifying the flow regime; using a model outside its domain of validity can still lead to poor predictions.
infographic.paper_title: AI Meets Turbulence Modeling: Complex Systems Perspective

title: Numerical Modeling of a Metallic Alloy Droplet Impact, Solidification, and Macrosegregation
authors: Ehsan Amani, Ali Moinirad
abstract: For the first time, we study the effects of mass transfer on alloy droplet impact, solidification, and solute non-homogeneity or MacroSegregation (MS). For this purpose, a multi-physics model, including fully-coupled hydrodynamics of multiphase flow, wetting, conjugate heat transfer, phase change, and mass transfer, is established and validated carefully across several benchmarks. In addition, a concentration-flux-correction algorithm is proposed to conserve the solute mass within the droplet at the numerical discretization level. The validated model is subsequently used to explore the impact and solidification of an alloy droplet. The results show that accounting for mass transfer and solute transport improves the prediction of the dynamics of a solidifying splat, in a consistent manner with experimental observations, while this effect has been neglected in all previous studies. The analysis demonstrates that this improvement results from the flow sensitivity to the mushy region thickness, which is regulated by local solute concentration through the solidus and liquidus temperatures. Furthermore, analyses of the MS map identify several critical segregation regions most susceptible to defect initiation, such as cracking, including a long negatively segregated vein within the lamella, formed by the severe advective flow through the mush in the middle stages of the impact, a positively segregated region near the rim of the splat, appearing as a result of hook formation, and a major positively segregated zone at the top of the rim, which develops following the accumulation of the solute-rich melt sustained by washout from the lamella.

infographic.key_insight: Including solute mass transfer in alloy droplet impact simulations changes the predicted solidification dynamics and reveals where macrosegregation forms during splat spreading and freezing.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The model improves prediction of solidifying alloy splats, which is important for controlling defects such as cracking in thermal spray and additive manufacturing processes.
method: Fully coupled multiphysics simulation of multiphase hydrodynamics, wetting, conjugate heat transfer, phase change, and mass transfer
Concentration-flux-correction algorithm to conserve solute mass at the discretization level
Validation against several benchmarks before applying the model to an alloy droplet impact case
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports careful benchmark validation and shows improved agreement with experimental observations when mass transfer and solute transport are included.
infographic.watch_item: Results depend on accurate mushy-zone thickness and solute transport modeling, so implementation details can strongly affect predicted segregation patterns.
infographic.paper_title: Numerical Modeling of a Metallic Alloy Droplet Impact, Solidification, and Macrosegregation

title: Partially-Averaged Navier-Stokes simulation of turbulent annular Poiseulle flow
authors: Li-Toong Yap, Marten Klein, Heiko Schmidt
abstract: Turbulent annular Poiseulle flow is commonly encountered in various engineering applications, such as heat exchangers. The effects of the inner wall transverse curvature on the flowfield, characterised by the ratio of inner and outer radii $η= R_{i}/R_{o}$, have been studied previously using Direct Numerical Simulations (DNS). Scale-resolving simulations based on a Reynolds-Averaged Navier Stokes framework offer a potentially cheaper alternative to traditional Large Eddy Simulations (LES); however it is not clear if such models are able to capture the turbulence anisotropy in the turbulent annular pipe flow. In the present study, turbulent annular Poiseulle flow at $Re_{D_{h}} = 8900$ is performed with the Partially-Averaged Navier Stokes (PANS) model, a variable-resolution turbulence model that is based on the conventional RANS modelling. The ability of the PANS model to capture the effects of the transverse wall curvature is found to be comparable with DNS and other RANS-based scale-resolving approaches despite its relative simplicity and reduced computational cost.

infographic.key_insight: PANS can capture the curvature-driven turbulence behavior in annular Poiseuille flow with accuracy comparable to DNS and other scale-resolving RANS approaches, while using less computational cost.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This makes PANS a promising lower-cost option for predicting turbulent flow in annular passages used in devices such as heat exchangers.
method: Simulated turbulent annular Poiseuille flow with the Partially-Averaged Navier-Stokes (PANS) model.
Targeted a Reynolds number of Re_Dh = 8900 and varied the inner-to-outer radius ratio η = Ri/Ro to assess transverse curvature effects.
Compared the PANS flowfield predictions against DNS and other RANS-based scale-resolving methods.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports that PANS captures the effects of inner-wall curvature and turbulence anisotropy with performance comparable to DNS and other scale-resolving approaches.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy depends on the chosen PANS resolution settings and model calibration, so validation is still needed before deploying it for new geometries or operating conditions.
infographic.paper_title: Partially-Averaged Navier-Stokes simulation of turbulent annular Poiseulle flow

title: CFD Forge: A Physics-Constrained Agentic Framework for Autonomous CFD
authors: Aakash Shailesh Oza, Ryan F. Johnson, Amir Barati Farimani
abstract: Setting up, running, and assessing a computational fluid dynamics (CFD) simulation requires substantial manual effort, from meshing and solver setup to diagnosis and interpretation, and repeating it across design variants slows engineering iteration. We present CFD Forge, an agentic framework built around OpenFOAM that carries an engineering request through case construction, meshing, solver execution, diagnostics, and reporting. A large language model interprets the request, reads the simulation evidence, identifies likely causes of problems, and proposes actions from a closed set. Automation is only useful if its results can be trusted, so acceptance is not left to the model: deterministic checks, registered for each type of flow, measure explicit criteria and decide. We demonstrate the framework on a converging-diverging nozzle and a two-dimensional forward-facing step, including geometry and operating changes requested in text. A turbulent cube, run outside the agent loop, shows why the checks matter: the solver completed and the mean drag settled, but the lateral-force oscillations were still growing, so a retrospective assessment withheld acceptance. To test this separation, we replayed 36 recorded simulation states, some with deliberately altered diagnostics, through the same model in two setups. Judging from the evidence without the check results, the model accepted 12 of the 13 detectable faults in all three repeats; with CFD Forge's checks deciding, none was accepted. The two setups also differ in prompting, and a fixed rule reached the same verdicts, so the model's value lies in the open-ended work rather than the verdict. Case files, recorded model calls, and decisions are retained for audit. A model that does the work, paired with checks that decide what is accepted, is a step toward automated CFD that can be trusted in high-throughput design and active-learning loops.

infographic.key_insight: CFD Forge combines an LLM-driven agent with deterministic, physics-based checks so the model can automate CFD workflows while fixed criteria decide whether results are accepted.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This can reduce manual effort in meshing, solver setup, debugging, and reporting for repeated CFD studies, making high-throughput design and active-learning loops more practical.
method: LLM interprets the engineering request and selects actions from a closed set for case construction, meshing, solver execution, diagnostics, and reporting.
Flow-specific deterministic acceptance checks evaluate explicit criteria and override model judgment when deciding whether a run is acceptable.
Validated on a converging-diverging nozzle, a 2D forward-facing step, and a turbulent cube retrospective test with recorded simulation states.
infographic.evidence_signal: In replay tests over 36 recorded simulation states, the model accepted 12 of 13 detectable faults when judging without check outputs, but accepted none when CFD Forge’s deterministic checks controlled the decision.
infographic.watch_item: Reliance on predefined check rules means coverage depends on how well each flow type’s acceptance criteria are designed and registered.
infographic.paper_title: CFD Forge: A Physics-Constrained Agentic Framework for Autonomous CFD

title: Wave-driven geostrophic vortices in rotating turbulence
authors: Vladimir Parfenyev, Sergey Vergeles
abstract: We perform direct numerical simulations of rotating turbulence to investigate the mechanisms responsible for the maintenance of large-scale geostrophic vortices. We confirm that the Reynolds stresses generated by inertial waves are consistent with the Reynolds-Averaged Navier-Stokes balance of the large-scale flow and demonstrate the predicted cyclone-anticyclone asymmetry, with cyclones exhibiting stronger azimuthal velocities and more compact cores. Wave-field analysis provides evidence that geostrophic vortices selectively reflect and absorb inertial waves according to the sign of their angular momentum. Wave absorption occurs either through the formation of a critical layer ahead of the reflection point or through enhanced viscous dissipation associated with increasing local wavenumber. As rotation increases, fewer inertial waves undergo resonant absorption, reducing angular-momentum transfer to the vortices and weakening the geostrophic flow. Consequently, the fraction of energy contained in geostrophic modes depends non-monotonically on the rotation rate, demonstrating that sufficiently rapid rotation can ultimately suppress, rather than enhance, turbulence two-dimensionalization.

infographic.key_insight: Geostrophic vortices in rotating turbulence are sustained by inertial-wave Reynolds stresses and selectively absorb waves by angular momentum sign, producing cyclone-dominated, non-monotonic two-dimensionalization at high rotation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This shows that increasing rotation does not always strengthen large-scale coherence, which matters for predicting mixing, energy transfer, and vortex formation in rotating machinery and geophysical flows.
method: Direct numerical simulations of rotating turbulence
Reynolds-averaged momentum balance to test large-scale geostrophic flow maintenance
Wave-field analysis of inertial-wave reflection, critical layers, and viscous absorption
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports DNS evidence that inertial-wave Reynolds stresses match the RANS balance, confirm cyclone-anticyclone asymmetry, and show a non-monotonic dependence of geostrophic energy on rotation rate.
infographic.watch_item: The conclusions depend on simulated rotating turbulence and may vary with Reynolds number, forcing, and domain geometry in practical systems.
infographic.paper_title: Wave-driven geostrophic vortices in rotating turbulence

title: Preferential concentration in a periodically forced particle-laden turbulent planar jet
authors: Mohammad Ahmad, Pierre Bragança, Christophe Cuvier, Martin Obligado
abstract: Periodic forcing is common in particle-laden jets, yet its influence on turbulence and inertial-particle clustering remains poorly understood. We investigate a turbulent planar jet at two Reynolds numbers, approximately 4950 and 9900 based on nozzle height, subjected to sinusoidal forcing at a frequency three orders of magnitude below the preferred jet instability. Hot-wire anemometry and high-speed particle imaging characterise the carrier turbulence, while Voronoi tessellations quantify preferential concentration of dilute inertial droplets. Despite its low frequency and moderate amplitude, forcing substantially modifies turbulence while leaving the mean-flow development nearly unchanged. The integral scale decreases by up to $40\%$, while forced and unforced jets retain the same time-averaged relationship between the dimensionless dissipation coefficient and Taylor-scale Reynolds number. Within the forcing cycle, velocity fluctuations and the Taylor microscale vary approximately in opposite phase, keeping the Taylor-scale Reynolds number within $\pm10\%$ of its cycle mean despite substantial variations in dissipation and Kolmogorov time scale. Particle clustering is even more sensitive, with forcing increasing mean preferential concentration and producing phase-dependent variations of $21$--$49\%$ of the cycle mean. Clustering peaks when the Kolmogorov time scale is largest, corresponding to the smallest particle Stokes number. Thus, markedly different clustering states occur at similar instantaneous Taylor-scale Reynolds numbers. These findings demonstrate that weak temporal modulation can control particle organisation without substantially altering the mean transporting flow.

infographic.key_insight: Weak sinusoidal forcing can strongly reshape turbulence and particle clustering in a planar jet even when the mean flow stays nearly unchanged.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Low-frequency modulation offers a practical control knob for tuning particle dispersion and preferential concentration in jet-based mixing, spray, and process-flow systems.
method: Hot-wire anemometry measured carrier-flow turbulence at two Reynolds numbers.
High-speed particle imaging and Voronoi tessellations quantified dilute inertial-particle clustering.
Forced and unforced jets were compared over the forcing cycle to track phase-dependent turbulence and Stokes-number changes.
infographic.evidence_signal: Experiments at nozzle-height Reynolds numbers of about 4950 and 9900 showed up to 40% reduction in integral scale and 21–49% cycle-mean variations in clustering, with clustering peaking when Kolmogorov time scale was largest.
infographic.watch_item: The forcing is weak and far below the jet instability frequency, so the results may not transfer directly to strongly forced or higher-concentration particle-laden flows.
infographic.paper_title: Preferential concentration in a periodically forced particle-laden turbulent planar jet

title: Gen-PINNs: Generative Adversarial Physics Informed Neural Networks for solving partial differential equations
authors: Muhammad M. Akmal, Kamy Sepehrnoori, Michael J. Pyrcz
abstract: Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) are a widely used data-free method for solving Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) using machine learning. With recent advances in Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), adversarial learning has shown strong capabilities for modeling complex data-driven problems; however, the use of GANs in deterministic physics-informed PDE solutions remains limited. In this work, we first identify limitations of standard PINNs for solving PDEs, including spectral bias, loss imbalance, and optimizer stagnation. We then propose Generative Adversarial Physics-Informed Neural Networks (Gen-PINNs), a unified deterministic residual-adversarial framework designed to improve data-free solutions of PDEs with sharp or shock-front behavior. The generator learns the underlying PDE solution using dynamically weighted physics-informed loss components, while separate discriminators evaluate complementary PDE residual features against ideal zero-residual states. The framework further develops and adapts several methodological components, including a Fourier representation for resolving high-frequency spatial content, an orthonormal spectral diagnostic for quantifying frequency-dependent solution errors, and a modified gradient-based dynamic weighting system for physics, initial-condition, boundary-condition, and adversarial loss objectives. Gen-PINNs is tested against standard PINNs on nonlinear and higher-order PDEs, including the Burgers, Allen-Cahn, and Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equations. The results demonstrate substantial improvements in accuracy and convergence across sharp-front, stiff, and higher-order PDE solutions, highlighting the potential of deterministic residual-adversarial learning as an effective approach for solving challenging nonlinear PDEs.

infographic.key_insight: Gen-PINNs combines physics-informed learning with adversarial residual discriminators to improve PDE solution accuracy, especially for sharp fronts, stiff dynamics, and high-frequency features where standard PINNs struggle.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This approach can make data-free simulation more reliable for nonlinear fluid and transport problems that require accurate resolution of shocks, interfaces, and multiscale structures.
method: Generator learns PDE solutions with dynamically weighted physics, initial-condition, and boundary-condition losses.
Separate discriminators judge residual patterns against an ideal zero-residual state.
Fourier-based representation and spectral diagnostics help capture and assess high-frequency behavior.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports testing on Burgers, Allen-Cahn, and Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equations, with improved accuracy and convergence over standard PINNs.
infographic.watch_item: The added adversarial and dynamic-weighting components may increase training complexity and require careful tuning for stable convergence.
infographic.paper_title: Gen-PINNs: Generative Adversarial Physics Informed Neural Networks for solving partial differential equations

title: On the relationships between pressure geometrization and vortex identification
authors: Han Tu, Hang Zhao, Qi Gao
abstract: The profound mathematical and conceptual analogy between pressure in fluid mechanics and gravity in general relativity motivates a novel geometric reinterpretation of flows. This article proposes a theoretical framework for geometrizing pressure by establishing a Newton-Cartan geometry and applying a conformal transformation to the spatial metric. The pressure field is reinterpreted as a geometric potential that induces an effective spatial curvature, encoded in the Ricci tensor Rij and the associated Einstein-like tensor Gij. Within this curved effective space, fluid particles under the exclusive influence of pressure follow geodesics, and the classical Euler equation is recovered in the weak-field limit. The pressure Poisson equation emerges naturally as a consequence of the geodesic equation and the Bianchi identity, revealing pressure as an instantaneous geometric constraint rather than an external force. This framework provides a unified geometric interpretation of widely used vortex identification criteria, demonstrating that the prevailing Eulerian and Lagrangian schemes correspond to different geometric invariants or projections of the effective curvature. In the degenerate two-dimensional (2D) limit, the effective spatial tensor vanishes identically, and the global integral of the total curvature vanishes as well. This topological constraint offers a novel interpretation of the dual-cascade scenario in 2D turbulence: the inverse energy cascade arises from geometric condensation of positive-curvature structures toward larger scales, while the forward enstrophy cascade results from geometric dispersion of negative-curvature structures toward smaller scales.

infographic.key_insight: Pressure can be treated as a geometric potential that curves an effective fluid space, making vortex-identification methods interpretable as curvature-based invariants.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This offers a unified mathematical lens for flow diagnostics and may improve how engineers interpret pressure-driven structures in turbulent and 2D flows.
method: Build a Newton-Cartan geometric framework for the flow field.
Apply a conformal transformation to map pressure into an effective spatial curvature.
Relate vortex criteria to Ricci/Einstein-like curvature tensors and geodesics.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract presents a theoretical derivation linking the geodesic equation, Euler equation, and pressure Poisson equation, but does not report numerical experiments or benchmark data.
infographic.watch_item: The framework is largely theoretical, so practical use will depend on how robustly the curvature-based quantities can be computed from noisy simulation or experimental data.
infographic.paper_title: On the relationships between pressure geometrization and vortex identification

title: Versatile two-layer model for thermohydraulic prediction of microchannel heat sinks
authors: Chih-Hsiang Chen, Kentaro Yaji
abstract: Three-dimensional conjugate heat-transfer simulations provide detailed predictions for microchannel heat sinks but can be computationally demanding when many geometries and operating conditions are evaluated. This study develops a versatile two-layer model (VTLM) that reduces the three-dimensional problem to two coupled two-dimensional fields while retaining the in-plane geometry of the flow passages and fins. Effects associated with the unresolved channel-height direction are incorporated through hydraulic and thermal closures that account for wall friction and the fluid- and fin-side contributions to interlayer heat transfer. The closures are evaluated from the representative channel geometry, flow-development condition, and fin configuration. The VTLM was assessed against three-dimensional reference models across broad ranges of channel aspect ratios and operating conditions, including uniform and nonuniform fin arrangements. Compared with the existing two-layer models, the VTLM showed improved overall agreement with the three-dimensional reference results. The results showed that prediction accuracy was governed mainly by the flow-development condition and channel aspect ratio, from which a conservative screening guideline was proposed for the examined straight-channel configurations. The assessment of finned expansion--contraction channels further supported the applicability of the VTLM to the investigated passages with abrupt width changes. Overall, the VTLM provides a reduced-dimensional framework for thermohydraulic analysis across the range of microchannel heat-sink configurations examined in this study without explicitly resolving the channel-height direction.

infographic.key_insight: A versatile two-layer model can replace expensive 3D conjugate heat-transfer simulations for microchannel heat sinks by capturing the in-plane geometry while modeling the channel-height effects with calibrated hydraulic and thermal closures.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This enables faster thermohydraulic screening of many microchannel designs and operating conditions, making geometry optimization and design-space exploration more practical.
method: Reduce the 3D heat-sink problem to two coupled 2D fields
Add closures for wall friction and interlayer heat transfer based on representative channel geometry and flow development
Retain fin and channel layout effects, including uniform and nonuniform fin arrangements
infographic.evidence_signal: The model was benchmarked against 3D reference simulations over broad ranges of aspect ratios and operating conditions, including finned expansion-contraction channels, and showed improved agreement over prior two-layer models.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy depends strongly on flow-development condition and channel aspect ratio, so the screening guideline should be applied cautiously outside the tested straight-channel configurations.
infographic.paper_title: Versatile two-layer model for thermohydraulic prediction of microchannel heat sinks

title: Physics Foundation Models for Efficient Control of Fluid Flows
authors: Mahindra Rautela, Shaifalee Saxena, Alexander Scheinker
abstract: We investigate whether a physics foundation model (PFM) pretrained for PDE forecasting can be repurposed for closed-loop fluid-flow control. We construct a PFM-based controller by attaching lightweight Gaussian actor and critic heads to frozen pretrained representations and train the policy using proximal policy optimization (PPO). We evaluate the approach on HydroGym's two-dimensional Kolmogorov-flow environment using vorticity observations at \(64\times64\) and \(128\times128\) resolutions and Reynolds numbers \(\mathrm{Re}=100\) and \(200\). Across these settings, we compare the frozen PFM controller against a baseline MLP policy trained with the same PPO framework. The PFM controller achieves consistently higher reward while requiring smaller executed action magnitudes over training, indicating improved control performance with reduced control effort. These results provide initial evidence that representations learned through self-supervised next-frame prediction can be transferred directly to closed-loop fluid flow control. Project page: https://mahindrautela.github.io/morph.

infographic.key_insight: A frozen physics foundation model pretrained for PDE forecasting can be repurposed into a stronger closed-loop fluid-control policy than a standard MLP using lightweight RL heads.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This suggests pretraining on general flow dynamics could reduce data and improve controller performance for practical active-flow control systems.
method: Freeze a PDE-forecasting physics foundation model and attach small Gaussian actor/critic heads.
Train the policy with proximal policy optimization (PPO) for closed-loop control.
Compare against an MLP policy under the same PPO setup on Kolmogorov-flow benchmarks.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluated in HydroGym’s 2D Kolmogorov-flow environment using vorticity at 64×64 and 128×128 resolutions for Re=100 and Re=200, where the PFM controller achieved higher reward with smaller action magnitudes than the MLP baseline.
infographic.watch_item: Results are limited to a specific 2D benchmark and frozen-representation setup, so transfer to more complex flows or real-world actuation remains unverified.
infographic.paper_title: Physics Foundation Models for Efficient Control of Fluid Flows

title: SAGE-PINN: A Singularity-free Axisymmetric Geometry-Encoded Physics-Informed Neural Network for Axisymmetric Multiphysics Flow in Cylindrical Coordinates
authors: Raj Maurya, Joyprakash Akhuli, Doyel Pandey
abstract: Physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) provide a mesh-free framework for multiphysics modeling, yet fluid flow in axisymmetric cylindrical coordinates remains largely unexplored because the governing operators are singular at the axis and momentum and energy are strongly coupled through advection and buoyancy. We introduce SAGE-PINN, a Singularity-free Axisymmetric Geometry-Encoded Physics-Informed Neural Network for this class of problems. SAGE-PINN removes the coordinate singularity by construction: the parity-preserving variable $s=r^2$ and a modified stream-function representation eliminate explicit $1/r$ terms from the trained residuals and satisfy mass conservation identically. Boundary-fitted analytical ansätze enforce the boundary conditions exactly, while staged momentum-thermal-joint training, residual normalization, Péclet- and Richardson-number continuation, and a physics-scaled drift guard stabilize the coupled optimization. The framework is trained without labelled data, using only physics and boundary constraints, and its predictions are validated against finite-element reference solutions for steady nanofluid flow and heat transfer through a stenosed artery over a wide range of flow and thermal regimes, without case-specific tuning. Mass conservation remains at single-precision round-off, and over the central operating range the axial velocity and temperature are reproduced within $1.6\%$ and $9.1\%$ relative $L_2$ error, respectively. The main deterioration occurs only in the limiting regimes of strongly buoyancy-influenced slow flow and highly advection-dominated heat transfer. Embedding cylindrical geometry, conservation structure, and boundary physics directly into the network provides a robust route to PINN simulation of axisymmetric multiphysics flows.

infographic.key_insight: SAGE-PINN encodes cylindrical axisymmetric geometry and conservation laws directly into a PINN to remove the axis singularity and model coupled flow–heat physics without labeled data.
infographic.engineering_relevance: It offers a mesh-free surrogate for stenosed-artery and similar axisymmetric multiphysics CFD problems, reducing the need for case-specific tuning while preserving mass conservation.
method: Uses the parity-preserving variable s=r^2 and a modified stream-function to eliminate explicit 1/r singular terms.
Enforces boundary conditions exactly with boundary-fitted analytical ansätze.
Stabilizes training with staged momentum-thermal-joint optimization, residual normalization, and Péclet/Richardson continuation.
infographic.evidence_signal: Validated against finite-element references for steady nanofluid flow and heat transfer, with mass conservation at round-off and central-range errors of 1.6% for axial velocity and 9.1% for temperature.
infographic.watch_item: Accuracy degrades in extreme regimes, especially strongly buoyancy-driven slow flow and highly advection-dominated heat transfer.
infographic.paper_title: SAGE-PINN: A Singularity-free Axisymmetric Geometry-Encoded Physics-Informed Neural Network for Axisymmetric Multiphysics Flow in Cylindrical Coordinates

title: Gas radiation and the gravity limit of flicker in a co-flowing hydrogen jet diffusion flame
authors: Tianfang Xie, Meng Wang
abstract: Although weak at normal gravity, gas radiation sets the gravity at which a co-flowing hydrogen jet diffusion flame stops flickering. Flamelet-based simulations with unity Lewis numbers, which reproduce the flicker frequency measured by femtosecond coherent anti-Stokes Raman scattering within 4%, are combined with local stability analysis. At one tenth of normal gravity, the adiabatic flame flickers, the radiating flame does not, and switching the emission off restores flicker. Radiation acts through two mechanisms that do not weaken at reduced gravity. The hot outer layer loses buoyancy in proportion to the gas residence time, and a disturbance that displaces the flame also displaces its emission, which damps the disturbance on the lean flank (displaced-emission damping). Freezing the radiative source, which removes only its response to disturbances, slows the downstream recession of the oscillation more than tenfold. Both mechanisms slow the upstream spreading of disturbances. This spreading, competing with the co-flow, sets the onset location and the critical co-flow. Without radiation, the spreading speed scales with the square root of gravity; its radiative reduction does not. At reduced gravity, the flicker limit therefore becomes a straight line relating the square root of the co-flow Froude number to a radiation number, the ratio of buoyant to radiative time scales. The calibrated line places the critical gravity for the experimental co-flow at 0.13 times normal gravity, 2.6 times the adiabatic value. It correctly predicted whether two further flames keep flickering. Beyond the limit, transient wave packets can mimic flicker throughout a short drop-tower test.

infographic.key_insight: Gas radiation, not just buoyancy, sets the gravity threshold for flickering in a co-flowing hydrogen jet diffusion flame by damping disturbance growth and shifting the critical co-flow condition.
infographic.engineering_relevance: For microgravity and reduced-gravity flame design, radiation must be modeled explicitly because it can suppress flicker and change flame stability predictions by factors of order unity.
method: Flamelet-based simulations with unity Lewis numbers reproduce measured flicker frequency within 4%.
Local stability analysis is used to separate buoyancy-driven and radiation-driven damping mechanisms.
A calibrated scaling law relates co-flow Froude number, gravity, and a radiation number to predict the flicker limit.
infographic.evidence_signal: The model matched femtosecond coherent anti-Stokes Raman scattering flicker frequencies within 4% and predicted the experimental critical gravity at 0.13 g, about 2.6 times the adiabatic limit.
infographic.watch_item: The calibrated criterion is demonstrated for a specific co-flowing hydrogen jet configuration, so extrapolation to other fuels, geometries, or strong nonequilibrium radiation conditions should be done cautiously.
infographic.paper_title: Gas radiation and the gravity limit of flicker in a co-flowing hydrogen jet diffusion flame

title: Planar intrusions from a narrow, jet-like source in a linearly stratified ambient
authors: Hai Duc Vu, Murray Rudman, Anja Slim
abstract: We present two and three dimensional direct numerical simulations of planar intrusions injected from a continuously supplied, narrow source into a linearly stratified ambient at the level of neutral buoyancy. The evolution passes through three phases. A laminar leading vortex dipole first advances at constant speed with a varicose wave train behind it; the trailing jet then undergoes a sinuous instability whose initial growth rate and wavelength agree with inviscid unstratified planar-jet theory evaluated on the local jet; the flow finally relaxes into a buoyancy-controlled wedge whose area grows linearly in time. Three-dimensional simulations show that the transition remains organized by the planar instability, while three-dimensionality reshapes the near-source region into a slowly evolving, actively mixing zone that entrains an additional twenty to one hundred percent of the source flux depending on source width. Rescaled with this measured effective flux, the downstream intrusion collapses reasonably well onto the similarity solution for a wide-source intrusion.

infographic.key_insight: A narrow jet injected at neutral buoyancy in a linearly stratified fluid evolves through a dipole-dominated start, a jet-instability transition, and then a buoyancy-controlled intrusion whose spread becomes self-similar after correcting for entrainment.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The results help predict and design mixing and spreading from narrow discharges in stratified environments such as outfalls, vents, and plume-based delivery systems.
method: 2D and 3D direct numerical simulations of planar intrusions from a continuously supplied narrow source
Tracked flow evolution across three regimes: leading vortex dipole, sinuous jet instability, and buoyancy-driven wedge growth
Compared instability growth and downstream similarity behavior against planar-jet theory and wide-source intrusion scaling
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports agreement with inviscid unstratified planar-jet instability theory, linear-in-time wedge area growth, and 3D entrainment increases of about 20% to 100% depending on source width.
infographic.watch_item: The downstream similarity collapse depends on a measured effective flux, so near-source 3D entrainment must be accounted for before applying the scaling.
infographic.paper_title: Planar intrusions from a narrow, jet-like source in a linearly stratified ambient

title: Embossing of Tapered, Isometric Micro-Interdigitated Flow Fields for Enhanced Desalination by Faradaic Deionization
authors: Md Habibur Rahman, Sadia Afrin, Kyle C. Smith
abstract: Engineered transport architectures can improve electrolyte distribution and active-material utilization in porous electrodes, yet their implementation remains limited by fabrication methods that compromise precision, throughput, active-material preservation, or scalability. Here, an integrated embossing-calendering method is introduced to pattern Prussian blue analog (PBA) porous electrodes with embedded, micro-interdigitated flow fields (e$μ$-IDFFs) for electrochemical desalination. This non-subtractive, roll-to-roll compatible method forms channels by controlling plastic deformation while simultaneously calendering the electrode, preserving active material and reducing patterning time by 100-fold relative to mechanical milling. Indentation experiments and a closed-form model further show that embossing requires 15-fold less force than stamping, while electrode microstructures show local densification beneath embossed channels. PBA electrodes are embossed with novel e$μ$-IDFFs that use continuous width-tapering with isometric flow paths that promote uniform electrolyte distribution, increase rate capability, and reduce polarization. Compared with e$μ$-IDFFs patterned using less scalable means and non-isometric flow paths, these e$μ$-IDFFs desalinate seawater-salinity feeds near to potable levels with 1.5-fold of its thermodynamic energy efficiency and water recovery. Brackish desalination benefits similarly. Tapered, isometric e$μ$-IDFFs and the embossing method introduced to pattern them are readily translated other electrochemical energy storage and separations systems.

infographic.key_insight: A roll-to-roll embossing-calendering process can rapidly pattern porous Prussian blue analog electrodes with tapered, isometric micro-interdigitated flow fields that improve electrolyte distribution and desalination performance.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The method preserves active material while enabling scalable, low-force fabrication of precision transport architectures for electrochemical separations and related porous-electrode devices.
method: Embossed channels into porous PBA electrodes by controlled plastic deformation during calendering.
Designed ebc-IDFFs with continuous width tapering and isometric flow paths.
Used indentation experiments and a closed-form model to quantify embossing force and local densification.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports ~100x faster patterning than mechanical milling, ~15x lower force than stamping, and desalination performance near potable levels with 1.5x thermodynamic energy efficiency and water recovery.
infographic.watch_item: Scalability is promising, but long-term durability and performance consistency under repeated roll-to-roll processing and real feed conditions still need validation.
infographic.paper_title: Embossing of Tapered, Isometric Micro-Interdigitated Flow Fields for Enhanced Desalination by Faradaic Deionization

title: One vertex generates the hard-sphere Boltzmann collision hierarchy
authors: I. Karlin
abstract: The Boltzmann equation is the fundamental kinetic bridge between molecular mechanics and fluid behaviour. It converts binary encounters into the evolution of a velocity distribution, underlies rigorous routes from hard-sphere dynamics to Euler and Navier--Stokes--Fourier equations, and remains indispensable when continuum descriptions fail, from hypersonic shock layers and atmospheric re-entry to rarefied multiscale flows. Yet its nonlinear collision term is conventionally represented by an infinite three-index tensor of collisional brackets, with apparently new coefficients at every polynomial order. Here we prove that this entire hard-sphere tensor contains only one primitive collision law: the exact rank-two stress-production vertex $S$. Every polynomial collision vertex is obtained from $S$ by a finite sequence of universal differential and tensor operations, and every conventional bracket follows by differentiation. Thus the interaction physics and its representation separate exactly: all hard-sphere-specific information is concentrated in $S$, whereas the hierarchy above it is universal algebra. A blind eighth-order test in a Mach-5 shock agrees with independent collision sampling and strongly amplifies a weak kinetic precursor. The hard-sphere hierarchy is infinite in dimension, but its primitive collision content consists of a single scalar law.

infographic.key_insight: The hard-sphere Boltzmann collision hierarchy can be generated from a single primitive rank-two stress-production vertex, S, rather than from many independent collision laws.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This reduces the apparent complexity of collision modeling and could simplify kinetic-based surrogates for rarefied-gas and high-speed flow simulation.
method: Proved that every polynomial collision vertex is derived from S via universal differential and tensor operations.
Showed that conventional collisional brackets follow by differentiation from the same primitive law.
Separated hard-sphere-specific physics from universal algebraic structure in the hierarchy.
infographic.evidence_signal: A blind eighth-order test in a Mach-5 shock matched independent collision sampling and amplified a weak kinetic precursor.
infographic.watch_item: The result is mathematically powerful, but practical use may depend on stable high-order differentiation and faithful numerical realization of the vertex-based construction.
infographic.paper_title: One vertex generates the hard-sphere Boltzmann collision hierarchy

title: Cova-PINN: Cross-Domain Conservation Physics-Informed Neural Network for Fluid-Solid Conjugate Heat Transfer in Complex Geometries
authors: Weizheng Zhang, Xunjie Xie, Hao Pan, Lin Lu
abstract: Multi-domain physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) flexibly model medium-specific representations to solve fluid--solid conjugate heat transfer (CHT). However, standard multi-domain PINNs enforce governing equations and interface conditions on separately sampled domain supports, which can yield plausible temperature fields but inaccurate end-to-end energy transfer and outlet temperatures. We propose Cova-PINN, a multi-domain PINN framework that aligns conservation support with thermal interaction paths in complex geometries. Cova-PINN jointly optimizes cross-domain composite control-volume balances at the local scale and paired-wall closure at the global exchanger scale. We evaluate Cova-PINN on four triply periodic minimal surface (TPMS) heat exchangers and a geometrically distinct DualMS design against CHT-specific, optimization-oriented, and complex-geometry PINN baselines under a common protocol. Relative to the closest baseline, MUSA-PINN-CHT, Cova-PINN reduces average outlet-temperature and device-level closure errors across the four TPMS topologies by $37.7\%$ and $60.2\%$, respectively, while also improving full-field and heat-duty accuracy, with consistent gains on DualMS.

infographic.key_insight: Cova-PINN improves fluid-solid conjugate heat transfer predictions by enforcing conservation across thermal interaction paths, not just within separately sampled fluid and solid domains.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This makes PINN-based surrogate modeling more reliable for heat exchanger design, especially when accurate outlet temperature and energy balance matter more than visually plausible temperature fields.
method: Uses a multi-domain PINN for fluid and solid regions in complex geometries.
Adds cross-domain composite control-volume conservation constraints at local scales.
Imposes paired-wall closure at the exchanger scale to preserve end-to-end heat transfer.
infographic.evidence_signal: Evaluated on four TPMS heat exchangers and a DualMS geometry, Cova-PINN outperformed multiple CHT, optimization-oriented, and complex-geometry PINN baselines, cutting average outlet-temperature error by 37.7% and device-level closure error by 60.2% versus the closest baseline.
infographic.watch_item: The added conservation constraints may increase implementation complexity and require careful balancing of local and global loss terms to avoid training instability.
infographic.paper_title: Cova-PINN: Cross-Domain Conservation Physics-Informed Neural Network for Fluid-Solid Conjugate Heat Transfer in Complex Geometries

title: Nonlocal generalization of the Chapman-Enskog method and hydrodynamic equations. Nonlocal vorticity transport in a turbulent medium
authors: A. B. Kukushkin
abstract: The results from [Fluid Dyn 61, 20 (2026)], concerning the generalized Chapman-Enskog method and a nonlocal (i.e., non-diffusive, spatially integral) viscous stress tensor in the Navier-Stokes equation, are extended to the case of arbitrary gradients of not only hydrodynamic velocity but also temperature. The resulting equations simplify the description of tangential discontinuities and separated flows. For the specific case of an incompressible medium, a nonlocal vorticity transport equation is derived that is structurally identical to the Biberman-Holstein equation for resonant radiation transport in plasmas and gases. A power-law form has been determined for the velocity distribution function of long-free-path vorticity carriers that satisfies empirical Richardson t^3 law for the mean square of relative separation of a pair of particles in a turbulent liquid or gaseous medium.

infographic.key_insight: The paper extends Chapman–Enskog theory to a nonlocal, spatially integral hydrodynamic closure that includes arbitrary velocity and temperature gradients, yielding a vorticity transport model analogous to Biberman-Holstein radiation transport.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This provides a more faithful continuum model for turbulent separated flows and tangential discontinuities, which could improve CFD treatments where local diffusion assumptions break down.
method: Generalize the Chapman–Enskog method beyond local gradient-based viscous stress.
Derive hydrodynamic equations with nonlocal stress and temperature-gradient effects.
For incompressible flow, formulate a nonlocal vorticity transport equation and identify a power-law carrier distribution consistent with Richardson's t^3 law.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract cites theoretical derivations and consistency with the empirical Richardson t^3 law, but does not report numerical experiments or benchmark data.
infographic.watch_item: The model is analytically appealing but may be difficult to calibrate and implement in practical CFD because the nonlocal kernel and carrier distribution are not yet validated against detailed experiments.
infographic.paper_title: Nonlocal generalization of the Chapman-Enskog method and hydrodynamic equations. Nonlocal vorticity transport in a turbulent medium

title: Preferential concentration of cloud droplets: Coupled effects of phase change and gravitational settling
authors: Zi-Mo Liao
abstract: Cloud droplets respond to turbulent motion with finite inertia and settle under gravity, while condensation and evaporation change their sizes. The nonuniform accumulation of cloud droplets in turbulent flows, known as preferential concentration, has attracted sustained interest because it affects droplet collision and coalescence rates. We develop an analytical theory that quantifies the coupled effects of droplet inertia, gravitational settling, and phase change on concentration changes. Applying this theory to simulations of two-dimensional homogeneous thermal convection reveals that phase change markedly enhances preferential concentration in this flow, primarily through spatial differences in settling speed. These differences arise because droplets experience different thermodynamic histories along their trajectories and thus acquire different sizes. Droplet transport further increases this settling contribution by rearranging droplets of different sizes. Fluid deformation partly offsets this enhancement by thinning concentration structures, reducing the preferential concentration measured at a fixed spatial scale.

infographic.key_insight: Phase change couples with inertia and gravity to intensify cloud-droplet preferential concentration by creating size-dependent settling differences along droplet trajectories.
infographic.engineering_relevance: This matters for cloud microphysics modeling because altered droplet clustering can change collision and coalescence rates, affecting precipitation formation predictions.
method: Developed an analytical theory for concentration changes in inertial droplets with gravity and phase change.
Decomposed preferential concentration into contributions from settling, droplet transport, and fluid deformation.
Applied the theory to 2D homogeneous thermal convection simulations.
infographic.evidence_signal: In the convection simulations, phase change markedly increased preferential concentration, with the strongest effect coming from spatially varying settling speeds caused by different thermodynamic histories.
infographic.watch_item: The enhancement is scale-dependent: fluid deformation can thin clustering structures and reduce the measured concentration at a fixed spatial resolution.
infographic.paper_title: Preferential concentration of cloud droplets: Coupled effects of phase change and gravitational settling
